name: REST
vendor: Architectural style (Roy Fielding, 2000); HTTP itself is an IETF standard
summary: The architectural style behind most HTTP APIs: resources with URLs, a few standard methods, status codes and cacheable responses, named by Roy Fielding in 2000.
intro: REST is a set of design constraints, not a protocol or a product. In practice a REST API is a set of URLs, each naming a resource (`/orders`, `/orders/4812`, `/orders/4812/items`), and clients act on them with HTTP methods whose meaning RFC 9110 fixes for everyone: `GET` and `HEAD` are safe, meaning they only read; `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent, so sending one twice has the same effect as sending it once; `POST` is neither. The server answers with a representation of the resource, usually JSON, and a status code: `2xx` for success, `3xx` for look elsewhere, `4xx` for the client’s mistake, `5xx` for the server’s. It keeps no session between requests: each one carries its own credentials and context, typically a token in the `Authorization` header, so any instance behind a load balancer can answer. Responses say how they may be cached. `Cache-Control: max-age=60` lets browsers, CDNs and proxies reuse a `GET` response for a minute; an `ETag` lets a client revalidate with `If-None-Match` and get an empty `304 Not Modified` when nothing changed, or update with `If-Match` and get `412 Precondition Failed` if someone else changed the resource first. Many APIs return errors as JSON in the `application/problem+json` format of RFC 9457.

Fielding’s definition asks for more than most APIs do. Its uniform interface includes hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS): responses carry links that tell the client what it can do next, so clients follow links instead of building URLs from documentation. Few public APIs work that way, and in 2008 Fielding wrote that an HTTP API not driven by hypertext “cannot be RESTful”. In everyday use, “REST API” means resource URLs, HTTP methods and JSON, with the rest (URL layout, pagination, versioning, error format) chosen by each API. Teams pin those choices down in an OpenAPI document, a YAML or JSON file listing paths, parameters, request and response schemas and auth schemes; version 3.2.1, published in September 2026, is current. Tools generate documentation, client SDKs and request validation from it, and Amazon API Gateway, Google’s API Gateway and Azure API Management can import it. There is nothing to buy: REST is a style, HTTP is an IETF standard, and the OpenAPI Specification is Apache 2.0-licensed.
strengths: Any HTTP client can call it: browsers, `curl`, every language’s standard library, with no code generation or translating proxy
HTTP infrastructure understands it: browsers and CDNs cache `GET` responses, load balancers and gateways route by method and path, and logs show readable URLs and status codes
Shared rules from the standard: safe and idempotent methods tell clients what they may retry, and status codes and conditional requests (`ETag`, `If-Match`) mean the same thing on every API
Statelessness makes scaling out simple: any server instance can answer any request
Mature tooling around OpenAPI: generated docs and SDKs, mock servers, request validation and gateway imports
limits: Over- and under-fetching: each endpoint returns a fixed shape, so a client gets fields it doesn’t need or makes several round trips to fill one screen, the gap that led Facebook to build GraphQL

No single standard: REST is a style, so URL layout, pagination, filtering, error bodies and auth differ from API to API, and every client learns each one afresh. An OpenAPI document records those choices; it doesn’t make them for you

Versioning is up to you, and large API publishers disagree: Google puts a major version in the path (`/v1/`), Azure requires an `api-version` query parameter, and GitHub uses a dated `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header

`POST` isn’t idempotent, so retrying a timed-out create can make a duplicate. An IETF draft for a standard `Idempotency-Key` header expired in 2026 without becoming an RFC; APIs such as Stripe’s define their own
Hypermedia is rarely implemented, so clients hard-code URLs and break when they move; by Fielding’s own definition most “REST APIs” are HTTP-based RPC

sections.title: What each HTTP method promises
sections.intro: These properties come from the HTTP standard (RFC 9110, and RFC 5789 for `PATCH`), so clients, proxies and caches can rely on them without reading your docs.

rows.label: `GET`
values: Read a resource or a list

rows.label: `HEAD`
values: Headers only: check existence, size or `ETag`

rows.label: `POST`
values: Only with explicit freshness and a matching `Content-Location`
Create in a collection, or run an action

rows.label: `PUT`
values: Create or replace at a known URL

notes: A successful `PUT`, `POST` or `DELETE` that passes through a cache makes it invalidate what it stored for that URL (RFC 9111).

sections.title: Three ways large APIs handle versions
sections.intro: REST leaves versioning to each API. Three of the biggest publishers picked three different places for the version.

items.name: Google
items.text: Every Google API has a major version number as the first part of the URL path, such as `v1`, with no minor or patch numbers; an incompatible change means a new major version.

items.name: Microsoft Azure
items.text: Every operation requires an `api-version` query parameter named by date, as in `PUT https://service.azure.com/users/Jeff?api-version=2021-06-04`; leaving it out returns `400`.

items.name: GitHub
items.text: Clients send an `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header with a date such as `2026-03-10`; requests without it get the `2022-11-28` version.

story: In 1993 the web was described by informal notes and draft specifications that, after Mosaic arrived, were far behind what browsers and servers actually did. Roy Fielding, a graduate student at UC Irvine writing the libwww-perl library, joined the standards work, co-authored the HTTP/1.0 specification with Henrik Frystyk Nielsen and became the primary architect of HTTP/1.1. Between October 1994 and August 1995 he worked out a model to explain how the web should behave while those specs were written. He first called it the “HTTP object model”, but people kept mistaking it for the design of an HTTP server.

His 2000 dissertation renamed it Representational State Transfer and built it up as a series of constraints: client and server, stateless requests, cacheable responses, a uniform interface, layers of intermediaries and optional code sent to the client. Each one gave up something, such as efficiency, for a property the web needed at internet scale.

The name was soon used for web APIs that used HTTP directly instead of SOAP envelopes; Amazon S3 launched in 2006 with both. By 2008 Fielding was “frustrated by the number of people calling any HTTP-based interface a REST API”. Swagger, created in 2010, became the OpenAPI Specification in 2015, and in 2022 RFC 9110, which Fielding co-edited, restated HTTP’s semantics.

choices.choice: A uniform interface instead of application-specific operations
choices.why: Fielding called it the central feature that distinguishes REST: the same few methods on every resource keep the architecture simple and let intermediaries see what each request does. He accepted that this “degrades efficiency”, since data moves in a standard form rather than one fitted to each application.

Each request must carry everything needed to understand it. That costs some repeated data per request but makes requests visible to monitors, failures easier to recover from, and servers quicker to free resources, so they scale.
A cache can reuse a response for later equivalent requests and skip some interactions entirely, cutting latency. The trade-off Fielding named is that a cache can serve stale data.

choices.choice: Layers that can’t see past their neighbours
choices.why: Proxies, gateways and shared caches can sit between client and server without either knowing. Layers add latency, but shared caches at organisation boundaries can more than make up for it.
